In [[mathematics]], a '''paramodular group''' is a special sort of [[arithmetic subgroup]] of the [[symplectic group]]. It is a generalization of the [[Siegel modular group]], and has the same relation to polarized [[abelian varieties]] that the Siegel modular group has to principally polarized abelian varieties. It is the [[automorphism group|group of automorphisms]] of '''Z'''<sup>2''n''</sup> preserving a non-degenerate skew-symmetric form. The name "paramodular group" is often used to mean one of several standard [[group representation|matrix representations]] of this group. The corresponding group over the [[real number|reals]] is called the '''parasymplectic group''' and is conjugate to a (real) symplectic group.  A '''paramodular form''' is a [[Siegel modular form]] for a paramodular group.

Paramodular groups were introduced by {{harvtxt|Conforto|1952}} and named by {{harvtxt|Shimura|1958|loc=section 8}}.

==Explicit matrices for the paramodular group==
There are two conventions for writing the paramodular group as [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]]. In the first (older) convention, the matrix entries are [[integer]]s but the group is not a subgroup of the symplectic group, while in the second convention the paramodular group is a subgroup of the usual symplectic group (over the [[rational number|rationals]]) but its coordinates are not always integers. These two forms of the symplectic group are conjugate in the [[general linear group]].

Any nonsingular skew-symmetric form on '''Z'''<sup>2''n''</sup> is equivalent to one given by a matrix
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} 0&F\\-F&0\end{pmatrix}</math>
where ''F'' is an ''n''-by-''n'' [[diagonal matrix]] whose diagonal elements ''F''<sub>''ii''</sub> are positive integers with each [[divisor|dividing]] the next.
So any paramodular group is conjugate to one preserving the form above, in other words it consists of the matrices
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}</math>
of GL<sub>2''n''</sub>&thinsp;'''Z''' such that
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}^t\begin{pmatrix} 0&F\\-F&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0&F\\-F&0\end{pmatrix}.</math>

The conjugate of the paramodular group by the matrix
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} I&0\\0&F\end{pmatrix}</math>
(where ''I'' is the [[identity matrix]]) lies in the symplectic group Sp<sub>2''n''</sub>&thinsp;'''Q''', since
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} I&0\\0&F\end{pmatrix}^t\begin{pmatrix} 0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} I&0\\0&F\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0&F\\-F&0\end{pmatrix}</math>
though its entries are not in general integers. This conjugate is also often called the paramodular group.

==The paramodular group of degree 2==

Paramodular group of degree ''n''=2 are subgroups of GL<sub>4</sub>&thinsp;'''Q''' so can be represented as 4-by-4 matrices. There are at least 3 ways of doing this used in the literature.
This section describes how to represent it as a subgroup of Sp<sub>4</sub>&thinsp;'''Q''' with entries that are not necessarily integers.

Any non-degenerate skew-symmetric form on '''Z'''<sup>4</sup> is up to [[isomorphism]] and scalar multiples equivalent to one given as above by the matrix
:<math>F=\begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\0&N\end{pmatrix}</math>.
In this case one form of the paramodular group consists of the symplectic matrices of the form
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} *&*&*&*/N\\ {}*&*&*&*/N\\ {}*&*&*&*/N\\ N*&N*&N*&*\end{pmatrix}</math>
where each <math>*</math> stands for an integer.
The fact that this matrix is symplectic forces some further congruence conditions, so in fact the paramodular group consists of the symplectic matrices of the form
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} *&N*&*&*\\ {}*&*&*&*/N\\ {}*&N*&*&*\\ N*&N*&N*&*\end{pmatrix}</math>
The paramodular group in this case is [[generating set of a group|generated]] by matrices of the forms
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} 1&0&0&0\\ {}0&1&0&0\\ {}x&Ny&1&0\\ Ny&Nz&0&1\end{pmatrix}</math> and <math>\begin{pmatrix} 1&0&x&y\\ {}0&1&y&z/N\\ {}0&0&1&0\\ 0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}</math>
for integers ''x'', ''y'', and ''z''.

Some authors use the matrix <math>F=\begin{pmatrix} N&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}</math> instead of <math>\begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\0&N\end{pmatrix}</math> which gives similar results except that the rows and columns get permuted; for example, the paramodular group then consists of the symplectic matrices of the form
:<math>\begin{pmatrix} *&*&*/N&*\\ {}N*&*&*&*\\ {}N*&N*&*&N*\\ N*&*&*&*\end{pmatrix}</math>
